hook.situation: You're lost at Seoul Station. You need the bathroom urgently, but the signs are all in Korean. You try 화장실 어디에요? — and a local points down the hall, speaks three fast sentences, and walks away. You caught the direction but not the words. What do you say next?
objectives: Ask where something is using 이/가 어디예요? and 이/가 있어요?
Use 부터/까지 to describe time ranges (9시부터 6시까지) and routes (여기부터 역까지)
Deploy repair phrases — 다시 말해 주세요, 천천히 말해 주세요, 잘 모르겠어요 — to keep conversations alive
hook.whyItMatters: Travel Korean lives or dies on two skills: finding things and recovering when you get lost in a conversation. 부터/까지 turns you from someone who can only ask about single moments ('몇 시에?') into someone who can talk about ranges ('여기서 거기까지 얼마나 걸려요?'). And the repair phrases are the difference between a Korean who keeps talking to you and one who switches to mime.

grammarNotes.title: 부터 / 까지 — From … to … (Ranges in Time and Space)
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of 부터/까지 as a RULER. Every ruler has a start end and a finish end. 부터 is the zero-end of the ruler — where you begin measuring. 까지 is the other end — where you stop. You can measure time (9시부터 6시까지 = 9 to 6) or space (여기부터 역까지 = from here to the station). A ruler without one end is fine — you can use just 까지 ('until 6') or just 부터 ('from 9 onward') — but using both creates the clearest picture.
grammarNotes.formation: Start-point + 부터 / End-point + 까지 (either or both, time or place)

examples.note: 두 끝 모두 사용 — both ends of the ruler used for a time range

examples.en: There's class from Monday to Friday.
examples.note: Days of the week can also be range endpoints — 부터 and 까지 work the same way

examples.en: I walk from here to the station.
examples.note: Space range: starting point (여기부터) + ending point (역까지)
Only the start end used — 부터 alone means 'starting from this point'

examples.en: How long does it take to Seoul Station?
examples.note: Only the end used — 까지 alone means 'as far as / all the way to'

contrastPairs.explanation: 에 pins a single moment — one tick on the clock. 부터/까지 draws a segment between two ticks. Use 에 for appointments ('meet me at 3'), use 부터/까지 for durations ('the shop is open from 10 to 9').

a.en: I go from home to school by bus.

b.en: From home to school by bus.

contrastPairs.explanation: For physical starting places, 에서 (집에서) is more natural than 부터 (집부터). 부터 works but sounds slightly unnatural for concrete departure points. 에서 = 'from' for places; 부터 = 'from' for time and abstract starting points. Both mean roughly the same here, but 에서 is preferred for locations.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'I go from school' uses 'from', which tempts learners to use 부터. But 부터 marks the starting point of a RANGE — it needs a destination (까지) or a specific context. '학교부터 가요' sounds like 'starting from school, I go' with no endpoint, which feels incomplete. Use 에 for simple destinations (학교에 가요 = go to school) or 에서 to mean 'departing from' (학교에서 출발해요).

exceptions: For physical locations as starting points, 에서 is more natural: 서울에서 부산까지 (from Seoul to Busan) is preferred over 서울부터 부산까지
오늘부터 (from today) and 지금부터 (from now) are extremely common fixed phrases — memorize both
까지 also means 'even' as an emphasis marker (너까지 = even you), which is different from the range meaning

grammarNotes.title: V아/어 주세요 — The Request Frame & Repair Phrases
grammarNotes.mentalModel: Think of V아/어 주세요 as a FAVOR TICKET. In Korean culture, asking someone to do something for you is phrased as asking for a favor (주다 = to give). You hand someone a ticket that says what action you want as a gift: '다시 말해' (say again) + 주세요 (please give me that) = 'Please give me the favor of saying it again.' Swap the verb before 주세요 and you get any polite request.
grammarNotes.formation: Verb stem + 아/어 주세요 (아 after ㅏ/ㅗ vowels, 어 after all others; 하다 → 해 주세요)

examples.note: 말하다 → 말해 주세요 — 하다 verbs become 해 주세요; 다시 means 'again/once more'
Same structure — add 천천히 (slowly) before the request to specify how
쓰다 → 써 주세요 — essential when you can't hear but can read
찍다 → 찍어 주세요 — tourist classic; mention what to photograph before the request
돕다 is irregular → 도와 주세요 / 도와주세요 (often written as one word) — survival phrase

contrastPairs.explanation: Without 주세요 the sentence is a statement or a command. Adding 주세요 reframes it as asking for a favor, which is much more natural and polite. Always use the 주세요 form when asking strangers.

b.en: Please wait a moment. (explicit polite request)

contrastPairs.explanation: 잠깐만요 is a quick pause signal — common but blunt. 기다려 주세요 explicitly asks for the waiting action as a favor, which is softer and clearer.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English speakers sometimes separate the adverb and add 주세요 at the very end after 요: '천천히 말해요 주세요.' But in Korean the verb form before 주세요 must be the plain stem form (말해), not the polite form (말해요). The 요 comes at the very end only once: 말해 주세요, not 말해요 주세요.

exceptions: 도와주세요 is almost always written as one word (not 도와 주세요), because 돕다 + 아/어 주세요 has become a fixed phrase
세요 (shorter form) is used with certain verbs: 앉으세요 (please sit), 오세요 (please come) — these are not V아/어 주세요 but honorific imperatives
주세요 can attach to nouns too: 물 주세요 = Please give me water (no verb stem needed when handing/giving is implied)

exampleSentence.note: 이 follows consonant-ending 실 — subject particle, not topic particle

exampleSentence.en: How long does it take to the subway station?
exampleSentence.note: 까지 = as far as / to — the end-point of a distance range
몇 번 = which number — essential for subway navigation

exampleSentence.en: I'll study hard starting from today.
exampleSentence.note: 부터 attaches to the start-point — 오늘부터 means 'from today onward'

extendedVocabulary.english: to / until / as far as (end point)

exampleSentence.en: Until what time are you open?
exampleSentence.note: 까지 after a time = 'until' — perfect for asking business hours
다시 placed before the verb — it modifies the action (말하다)
천천히 before 말해 주세요 specifies the speed — add it any time you need less pace
잘 모르겠어요 is softer and more natural than just 몰라요 — 겠 adds an element of 'I think / I guess'

exampleSentence.en: I walk from here to the station.
exampleSentence.note: 걷다 is ㄷ-irregular: 걷 + 어 → 걸어요 (ㄷ changes to ㄹ before a vowel)
얼마나 걸려요? (How long does it take?) is a must-know travel question — 걸리다 expresses time cost
돕다 + 아/어 주다 → 도와주다 (ㅂ-irregular): 도와주세요 is a one-word survival phrase

exampleSentence.en: I'm looking for the subway station.
exampleSentence.note: 찾고 있어요 = currently searching (ongoing action) — useful when you're lost and need help

exampleSentence.en: It's a 10-minute walk from here to the station.
exampleSentence.note: 여기부터 = starting from here — pairs naturally with 까지 for distance ranges

extendedVocabulary.english: over there (that place in the distance)

exampleSentence.note: 저기 = yonder/over there (visible but farther away). 여기 = here, 거기 = there, 저기 = over there
으로 = direction marker (go via/toward). 왼쪽으로 가다 = go left

exampleSentence.en: There's a convenience store on the right.
exampleSentence.note: 에 있다 = something exists in that location — combine direction + 에 있다 to describe where things are
알겠어요 is warmer and more engaged than just 네 — it shows you actually processed what was said

extendedDialogue.setting: Jimin is a foreign learner at Seoul Station. She approaches 민준 (a station employee) looking confused.

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.en: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
lines.grammarNote: 저기요 = 'hey' / 'excuse me' to get attention. 화장실이 어디예요? — 이 is the subject particle after consonant-ending 실; 어디 = where

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.en: Go toward exit 3. It's on the right.
lines.grammarNote: 쪽으로 = toward (that direction). 오른쪽에 있어요 = exists on the right side — 있어요 + 에 for static location

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.ko: 죄송한데, 천천히 말해 주세요. 잘 이해가 안 돼요.
lines.romanization: joesonghande, cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo. jal ihaega an dwaeyo.
lines.en: Sorry, please speak slowly. I don't understand well.
lines.grammarNote: 천천히 말해 주세요 — V아/어 주세요 request pattern; 잘 이해가 안 돼요 = 'understanding doesn't work well' — natural way to say 'I don't get it'

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.ko: 아, 네! 저기 계단 보여요? 계단에서 오른쪽으로 가세요.
lines.romanization: a, ne! jeogi gyedan boyeoyo? gyedaneseo oreunjjogeuro gaseyo.
lines.en: Ah, yes! Do you see those stairs over there? From the stairs, go right.
lines.grammarNote: 계단에서 오른쪽으로 가세요 — 에서 marks the starting point of the movement (stairs → go right from there)

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.ko: 알겠어요! 감사합니다. 혹시 지하철 2호선은 몇 번 출구예요?
lines.romanization: algesseoyo! gamsahamnida. hoksi jihacheol 2-hoseon-eun myeot beon chulguye yo?
lines.en: Got it! Thank you. Also, which exit is Subway Line 2?
lines.grammarNote: 알겠어요 = 'I understand' (genuine comprehension). 몇 번 = which number — essential number-question for subway exits

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.romanization: 2-hoseon-eun 5beon chulguye yo. yeogiseo 5beon chulgukka ji georeoseo 3bunieyo.
lines.en: Line 2 is exit 5. It's a 3-minute walk from here to exit 5.
lines.grammarNote: 여기서 5번 출구까지 — 에서 marks departure point; 까지 marks arrival point; 걸어서 = 'by walking / on foot'

lines.speaker: 지민
lines.romanization: 2-hoseon-eun myeot sibuteo myeot sikkaji unhaengha eyo?
lines.en: From what time to what time does Line 2 operate?
lines.grammarNote: 몇 시부터 몇 시까지 — RULER pattern for asking time ranges; 운행하다 = to operate/run (for transportation)

lines.speaker: 민준
lines.romanization: 5si 30bunbuteo jajeongkkaji unhaengha eyo. oneulbuteo iyonghae boseyo!
lines.en: It runs from 5:30 to midnight. Start using it from today!
lines.grammarNote: 5시 30분부터 자정까지 — complete ruler range with both endpoints; 오늘부터 이용해 보세요 = 'try using it from today' — V아/어 보세요 = 'try doing'

readingText.title: 서울역에서 온 문자 (Text messages from Seoul Station)
readingText.body:
지민: 민아야, 지금 서울역에 있어. 근데 길을 잘 모르겠어.
민아: 어디 가려고?
지민: 2호선 타려고. 몇 번 출구인지 몰라.
민아: 14번 출구야. 거기서 2호선 홈까지 걸어서 5분이야.
지민: 아, 그리고 화장실도 찾고 있었는데.
민아: 화장실은 1번 출구 왼쪽에 있어. 출구에서 나오면 바로 보여.
지민: 알겠어! 참, 이 역 몇 시까지 열어?
민아: 서울역은 아침 5시부터 자정까지 열어.
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jimin: Mina, I'm at Seoul Station now. But I don't really know my way around.
Mina: Where are you trying to go?
Jimin: I'm trying to take Line 2. I don't know which exit it is.
Mina: It's exit 14. From there to the Line 2 platform is a 5-minute walk.
Jimin: Oh, and I was also looking for the bathroom.
Mina: The bathroom is to the left of exit 1. Once you come out the exit, you'll see it right away.
Jimin: Got it! By the way, until what time is this station open?
Mina: Seoul Station is open from 5 AM to midnight.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Which exit should Jimin use to get to Line 2?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 14번 출구 (exit 14). From there it's a 5-minute walk to the Line 2 platform.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Where is the bathroom?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 1번 출구 왼쪽에 있어 — it is to the left of exit 1, visible as soon as you exit.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every use of 부터 and 까지 in the text. Why is each one used — and why does one sentence use both?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 몇 시까지 열어? — 까지 alone marks the end-point of the opening hours (asking 'until what time'). 아침 5시부터 자정까지 열어 — both 부터 and 까지 appear because Mina is giving the full range: 'from 5 AM (부터 = start) to midnight (까지 = end)'. The first question only needed the endpoint; the answer needed both endpoints of the ruler.

culturalNote.title: 역 문화 — Subway Station Culture in Korea
culturalNote.body: Seoul's subway is one of the world's most navigated systems, and Korean stations are built around the assumption that you might not know where you are. Every exit is numbered (1번 출구, 2번 출구…), and Koreans give directions by exit number — not left or right from the entrance. So when someone says '2호선은 5번 출구예요,' they expect you to find exit 5 on the station map and orient from there. Station staff (역무원) are trained to help and are very patient with foreigners — they will often walk you part of the way. Don't be shy about using 다시 말해 주세요 or 천천히 말해 주세요. Korean station staff hear these phrases from tourists every day, and asking for a repeat is far more respected than nodding and wandering off confused.

inlineExercises.explanation: 부터 marks the start-point (9시부터 = from 9) and 까지 marks the end-point (6시까지 = to/until 6). 에 alone (9시에 / 6시에) would give two single time-points but not express a range. 에서 is for places where actions happen, not time expressions.
The V아/어 주세요 pattern uses 주세요 (from 주다 = to give, as a favor). 말해요 alone is a statement ('you say it again'). 주어요 is not a polite request form — 주세요 is the standard polite imperative of 주다.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '여기부터 역에서 걸어요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 에서 marks where an action happens (a stage), not a destination endpoint. The ending point of a range takes 까지 — '역까지' means 'all the way to the station.' 역에서 걷다 would mean 'walking at the station' (action happening there), not 'walking as far as the station.'

inlineExercises.prompt: A local just gave you fast directions. You didn't catch everything. What do you say?
inlineExercises.explanation: 천천히 말해 주세요 (Please speak slowly) is the best repair phrase when the issue is speed. 잘 모르겠어요 (I don't really know) signals confusion but doesn't ask for help. 다시 한 번 주세요 is missing the verb — it would mean 'give me one more time' (like asking for a second serving). 네, 알겠어요 would falsely signal comprehension.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'From Monday to Friday there is class.'
inlineExercises.hint: Which particle marks the start of a range? Which marks the end? What pattern says 'there is'?

inlineExercises.prompt: 죄송한데, 천천히 말해 ___ . (Sorry, please speak slowly.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 말해 주세요 = the complete V아/어 주세요 request form. 말해요 alone = a statement or direct command, which would sound rude to a stranger. 주다 is the infinitive/dictionary form — you cannot end a polite sentence with a bare infinitive.

inlineExercises.prompt: 역 사무소는 오전 9시___ 오후 6시___ 열어요. Which pair of particles fits?
inlineExercises.explanation: This is a time range (opening hours), so you need the RULER pair: 부터 for the start (9시부터) and 까지 for the end (6시까지). 에 alone marks single moments, not ranges. 에서 is for physical locations where actions happen, not time expressions. Mixing 에서 or 에 with 까지 would be grammatically wrong here.

bullets: 부터/까지 = the RULER: draw a line between a start (부터) and end (까지) for time ranges and routes — 9시부터 6시까지, 여기부터 역까지
V아/어 주세요 = the FAVOR TICKET: swap any verb in front of 주세요 for any polite request — 말해 주세요, 써 주세요, 찍어 주세요
Repair toolkit: 다시 말해 주세요 (again), 천천히 말해 주세요 (slowly), 잘 모르겠어요 (I'm not sure) — use these freely and Koreans will respect you for it
summaryCard.nextChapterTeaser: Next up: Chapter 11 introduces wants and plans — 싶다 (want to), -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (going to / planning to). You'll go from asking where things are to expressing what you want to do there.
